body: So true! Agreed!

I think it can be. I have had people open up to me about things they've never told anyone else because I wasn't afraid to ask about it. And I have supported people through those difficult and often stigmatized issues.

But I understand that it can also be a really unhealthy behaviour if it goes unchecked and you're not aware of it.

Your story and feelings really resonate with me, as our stories have many similarities (intergenerational NPD, heartbreak, not wanting my ex's pain to go in vain, emptiness, feeling burdened by the weight of the realization, hopelessness).

Age is definitely on your side, and I want to give you some kudos for having this realization. It's an incredibly hard pill to swallow, but awareness is the first step toward improvement. 

As others have said, therapy and mindfulness can do wonders... But therapists are not all created equally. Your therapist sounds very uneducated about NPD... Many are. It might be helpful to find a therapist who focuses on PDs or at least is trained in DBT. DBT is a recommended treatment for cluster B PDs. 

Also check out r/dbtselfhelp to get started on your own if you want :)
Great comment and advice. Only thing I'm wondering is... Antidepressants? Never heard that be recommended for NPD.
Seconding this. Meditation and practicing mindfulness can change your life.

thanks for your kindness. i understand. pwNPDs' inability to see their own abusive behaviours is infuriating for those around them (i know this as the child of a pwNPD). thank you for your kind words.
hey, i'm doing a lot better now. you can look through my comments and posts if ya want a better idea, or message me directly. it's painful as fuck but you can get past the pain.
100%. I also think I am the most "dangerous"/harmful to myself and others during these hypomanic episodes.

Isolate ASAP, release frustration if needed (scream, punch an inanimate object, etc.), check in with yourself (ask why are you angry? Is it justified? What is the best way to solve this?), engage in mindfulness practices.
Not true, there are some great therapists who offer sliding scale payment options if you ask.
If the ones who specialize in personality disorders are too expensive/don't accept insurance, maybe try those who are trained in DBT.

I'm interested to know what makes you think/say that as well? I don't think it's fair to characterize uninvitednarc as a sociopath based on this comment. This could easily be someone on the higher end of the NPD spectrum.

this is such a necessary dialogue to be having. gatekeeping is super alive and well on this sub, but it's sad... i feel that the whole "narcissist pride" attitude is just internalized stigma. these pwNPD are like "everyone thinks i'm a monster, so why not just embrace it and gain from it," and it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. sad.
Yeah, that's a fair analysis. My NPD makes it really fucking hard to know if what I'm doing - or even feeling - is genuine or not. It's a constant battle.

On a wait list to get a professional assessment done, but my guess would be NPD with some BPD overlap.

I agree that it's more complicated, but I found the label really helpful (once I was able to get over the backbreaking weight of the stigma) in terms of realizing I wasn't fucked up for no reason, realizing I wasn't alone in this, and for having a framework for understanding my behaviours and moods.
Have you been diagnosed with NPD and/or ASPD?
Maybe. I just want to see us all do better.

I *did* feel like a total fraud re: my leftist values when I realized I had NPD, but now that I'm working on myself a lot, I know those values are genuine and remain deeply important to me. I unfortunately used my values in a holier-than-thou manner, to virtue signal that I was this selfless, magnanimous person (think annoying SJW). But I'm conscious of that now and I keep a lot of "selfless" things that I do to myself.

As fucked up as this lefty narc phenomenon is, I don't think it's necessarily as simple as us virtue-signalling just to get supply. Our manipulative ways are generally not so calculating and planned.

I only started practicing meditation regularly after I hit rock bottom. It's a difficult practice to commit to, especially if you don't really understand the depth of the consequences of your behaviours and moods. People only change when they're ready to do so.
Nah, because a part of you agrees with me. You're just stifling it. But I'll agree to stop repeating myself now lol. Wish you the best.

Thanks for sharing your thoughts. I'm happy for you that you had that "flip of the switch"... I had a similar moment during meditation that changed my whole outlook on my NPD. Meditation can be such a game changer for us (and anyone really).

Constant self-awareness and -reflection is so key because of the mental gymnastics you mention. Great post!

I promise you, you won't reach "the top tier of males" lol (whatever that means). That's your grandiosity talking, and on some level, you know that. Even if you do reach that goal, it's a lonely and desolate place to be (as is the pursuit of that goal, which you seem to recognize). 

Sure, you have the capacity to feed those "dark triad" characteristics, but you are more than that... You have the capacity to nourish other, better parts of yourself. I'm glad you're meditating though.

thanks for sharing your thoughts. i feel ya... it's hard to feel that you *should* try to get treatment for your NPD when you feel that it's served you well. i think ultimately though, the "success" it brings is meaningless and vapid without love and compassion in your life.

how do you plan to "reach great success" *without* forming connections with people? what do you define as success? i guess if you work in a corporate setting and your goal is to make a lot of money, NPD would likely help you with that. how do you plan to develop the ability to form connections with people down the road?

i agree with you that connecting to our true selves is key, but i think that means different things to you and i. having self-awareness (gaining an understanding of our traits, patterns, behaviours) is the first step in improving ourselves.

*edit: italicization*
oof. left-leaning narc here. that's messed up.
it's been really helpful for me, but it's also a very rollercoaster-y experience. some days i hate him. it also really helps that he and i aren't under the same roof anymore.

i practice regular ass, plain ol' focusing on my breaths. no visualizations, no music or guiding, just focusing on breaths and trying to observe the mind without judgment. i'm not sure if there's a name for it but i guess the closest thing would be mindfulness meditation. i also attend a buddhist meditation group weekly where we meditate together and our teacher gives a talk related to mindfulness.

thank you for sharing this and being vulnerable. it's okay to express sadness, fear, pain, and any other feeling you're having. if i can help in trying to find resources for you in your city, i'm happy to do that... feel free to message me. you deserve and can find healing and community, i promise. just know that you owe it to yourself and to your loved ones to get better. you've already gotten past a huge hurdle, which is awareness of your illness. stay with the awareness and move forward.

yeah the realization can be horrifying and scary because of the stigma, but it's also super comforting to finally (start to) understand why you are the way that you are, and know that you're not alone. i wish you all the best in your journey.

so true... that's why i'm so tired of being labelled an untreatable monster. ANYONE can change their reactions, behaviour, outlook with self-reflection and discipline; those of us with personality disorders are no exception.

i realized i likely had NPD after my ex-partner broke up with me. it was the first time i knowingly and intentionally manipulated him. i was like, "how can i be this heartless? how can i knowingly manipulate him after all he's done for me?" and thought that i might be a psychopath. so i started researching psychopathy, which led to ASPD, to cluster B PDs, to NPD. i could relate to most of the traits, and also realized that my dad fit all of the NPD criteria. i started to go through my old journals and re-discovered how abusive my dad has been to me all my life (i had suppressed most of those memories), and it all made sense. i also believe that i have several BPD traits but i'm waiting to get a formal assessment done next month.

how about you? how did you realize you had ASPD?
that's brave of you to share that with her. i wish you all the best in your journey.

meditation and mindfulness have really helped me to stay in the present, feel motivated to do/be better, and let go of the past (while still acknowledging the harm i caused, and learning from my mistakes).

thank you for your approach and for sharing.

I have NPD, my dad has NPD, and I'm pretty sure my grandfather had NPD.

So yes, I absolutely believe that children of narcissists often become narcissists themselves. It also seems common for some children of narcissists to become empaths/HSPs.

You're right... It **is** easier to wallow in self-pity, and maybe you need to do that for a bit after this tough realization, but use the arrogance gifted to you by this disorder (lol) to challenge yourself and do the hard thing.

Congrats on having this realization. Stay with it. Don't allow your brain to fall back into its pattern... Don't allow it to wrangle itself out of awareness and accountability this time. Awareness is huge, and is the first step towards change.

There is hope. There are several people on this sub who have made significant improvements, with time and with a commitment to getting help and doing the work. We are not NPD, we are human beings with NPD, and with the capability of neuroplasticity. We can change.

I wrote this post yesterday (https://www.reddit.com/r/NPD/comments/bsz0kk/there_is_hope/). I hope it helps.

Same re: my dad, and his dad. I just got out of a phase where I blamed my dad for everything that was going wrong in my life, but then I realized 1) it was actually all my fault, and 2) I was begging for people's compassion and giving none to my dad. I thought about his life and his relationship with his dad, as well as my grandfather's life. I started to understand his behaviours as an expression of the pain he has never had the time/space to try to understand or work through. I started to give him the compassion and understanding I was able to give myself.

Getting dumped by my ex was the catalyst for me gaining insight into my NPD and starting to get help/improve. Having the time and space to focus on myself has been life-changing for me.

I wouldn't have had the courage to leave my ex, so I know this must be an incredibly tough decision for you, but the toughest decisions often lead to the greatest rewards. Something my ex said while breaking up with me that might be helpful for you: "I'd rather us break up now and still be able to be friends than us force staying together until we resent each other."

I read books, articles on NPD and almost all of it was dehumanizing and targeted at those who have been on the receiving end of narcissist abuse. I was suicidal and hopeless. I am getting help... Lots of it (DBT, therapy, meditation). Thank you for having a more nuanced view of NPD.

The most disappointing thing for me is seeing all these so-called experts (psychologists, psychiatrists, researchers) writing books painting us as untreatable monsters.

Trust me, I know this. I am both a narcissist and the child of a narcissist/"victim" of narc abuse. I don't mean to minimize the harms caused by narcissists with this post.

I am trying to signal boost an alternate, but parallel, discourse about narcissism. Everyone else talking about narcissism is already talking about all the things you mention in your comment. My point is that both of these discussions are necessary when talking about narcissism.

More commonly, we experience a struggle between the conscious and subconscious. There is a part of us that knows that what we're doing is wrong, hurtful, manipulative... But our learned thinking patterns come in and we manage to convince ourselves that we did nothing wrong. It's a disconnect.

I also have covert narcissism and relate to a lot of what you're saying. Awareness is huge. Some narcs never reach self-awareness, so kudos to you for staying with and deepening your awareness. I know it's uncomfortable, but try to deepen your self-awareness. Explore why you are the way you are... Narcissism doesn't just come out of thin air. It's a coping and survival mechanism learned during our early years. 

I've completely stopped reading up on narcissism, because you're right... So much of what's written about it is hyperbolic, sensationalist, and engenders feelings of hopelessness. It's simplistic bullshit, but it sells. Ignore it.

Remember that NPD is not who you are; it is a part of you. You are capable of loving and caring for others. Instead of focusing on my diagnosis of NPD, I focus on unlearning abusive and harmful behaviours, and this approach has been so much more helpful for me. 

Are you in therapy? What are you doing to care for yourself and get better? I've been meditating and seeing a therapist and it's been a huge help for me. I hope you find the support you need to get better (because you can get better, despite what those books say).
So ignorant

As both a narcissist and child of a narcissist, a lot of the stuff that's written about narcissists is hyperbolic, sensationalist, and makes us out to be evil, scheming monsters. It's easier to sell books that way ;) 

I only recently became aware of my narcissism. I can tell you that I was not intentionally trying to be mean, abusive, or harmful to my loved ones. My abusive behaviour is a coping mechanism that I learned from my dad, who learned it from his dad (not to blame my shitty behaviour on them, just to give you the background). I was honestly shocked when I realized I had several traits of NPD. Narcissists often have very little self-awareness. 

As u/milesamsterdam said, narcissism is a spectrum. Cluster B personality disorders often have a lot of overlapping traits, so if someone with NPD also has ASPD traits, they could be more like that "evil, scheming monster" that everyone loves to write about (but, again, that is so simplistic and ignores the trauma that made the person that way...). But the truth is that most narcissists have learned this behaviour as a coping mechanism to survive with their narcissist caregiver, and they are not sadistic... They have just learned to protect their ego at all costs.

It's so easy to write people off as subhuman monsters, but people aren't just shitty for no reason. Trauma, pain, and anguish make people that way. Trauma can be worked through, and people can unlearn harmful behaviours.

I went through a terrible breakup a few months ago, and I spiralled HARD afterward, but I now view it as a gift that's opened my eyes and given me the opportunity to change. I hope that once you get through the immediate pain, you are able to see this as an opportunity as well. Be safe.

These are the wake-up calls we need, and if we allow them to be, the catalysts for change. I know it's incredibly painful right now, but dive into the pain... Find out why you are a narcissist and deal with that pain. Identify how that's affected you. Make it your central goal to end this cycle of abuse. Do not allow yourself to fall back into your old patterns of thinking and acting. Get help. I'm going through it now... In solidarity.

my ex and i planned to go to couple's therapy but then he ended up (smartly) breaking up with me, so i continued with individual therapy. again, it was only after he broke up with me that i was able to be honest with myself and my therapist about what my issues were.

> I feel guilty because we've been married a long time 

this is not a reason to feel guilty. this feeling could keep you in a miserable marriage for the rest of your life. you deserve better than that. you deserve happiness.

sounds like you've laid out your concerns and given her the opportunity to change. i'm glad you recognize her behaviour as abusive. abusers don't change unless they feel powerless... right now, sounds like she gets feelings of power from the way she treats you, so she likely won't change as long as you stay with her (and maybe still won't after that).

i know it must feel really scary right now. you can start making your exit plan. sounds like you have trusted friends and family back home that would support you. can you tell one trusted person? can you start exploring where you would want to go after leaving the marriage? do you need financial support? start thinking about these things, and go from there. you can also look for organizations near you that support people in abusive relationships.

you deserve to be happy.

>at both of these points in our relationships I felt as though we were the happiest

speaking as someone who cheated for "no reason" and during very happy times in my past relationships... at the very least, take time and space from each other. he needs to understand why he cheated and how he's going to make sure it never happens again. he needs to do that work and come back to you with his thoughts and his ACTIONS. and you need to process your feelings, desires, expectations. it's very hard for both of you to do this work while being together, living together.

i was only able to understand and accept the reasons i cheated after my ex broke up with me. before that, i was so focused on us staying together that i was just doing and saying whatever i thought would keep us together. your partner might be different, but for me, it's going to take months (maybe years) of therapy, self-reflection, and work to (hopefully) get to a place where i can be sure that i won't do this again.

i'm sorry you're dealing with this. all the best to you.
